title: More Than a Symptom
paragraphs: Few paintings are as widely reproduced as The Starry Night, and fewer still are as widely misdescribed. This essay argues for a different emphasis. It is frequently presented as the spontaneous outpouring of a troubled mind, a view that flatters our taste for romantic legends but fits the evidence poorly.

The Museum of Modern Art, which owns the canvas, offers a more careful account. Van Gogh painted it in mid-June of eighteen eighty nine, in the course of roughly twelve months spent at the Saint-Paul-de-Mausole asylum in Saint-Remy, where he had sought relief from his mental illness. The composition was inspired by the view from his window but depends equally on imagination, memory and emotion. The asylum years were difficult, yet they were also productive, and the two facts should be held together.

That blend is the key to its effect. The village beneath the sky is not a record but an invention, and the cypress that rises in the foreground behaves less like a tree than like a gesture. Even the celebrated sky, with its thick swirling strokes, seems to record how the night felt rather than how it looked. Such choices are the signature of a painter in command of his material.

Why does the distinction matter? If we read the painting as a symptom, we reduce deliberate artistic choices to an accident of illness. If, instead, we read it as a composition, we can admire the control behind the apparent turbulence. The second reading respects both the artist and the work. That is a more generous and a more accurate way to look.
None of this denies that Van Gogh suffered. It simply insists that suffering does not explain skill, and that the sky we admire was made by a painter thinking as hard as he was feeling.
